findings.title: Redirect-follow loop bound cut 10x with no rationale; warning comment deleted
findings.body: The Lua `for i = 0, 10000 do` bound for resolving parent redirects was reduced to `for i = 0, 1000 do`, and the comment that explicitly documented the consequence ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted in the same change. With the new bound, segment trees whose redirect chain is longer than 1000 will silently stop being joined: the loop exits while `new_set_span` is still a different key, the final `hset` then writes a wrong redirect, and subsequent spans get routed into the wrong set instead of being merged. This is a data-integrity regression that should either be reverted or come with an explicit justification for why a shallower limit is now acceptable.

findings.title: Unrelated OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-logs branch added to a spans-buffer PR
findings.body: The PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and the description is just "Test 2", yet the diff also introduces an entirely new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (paginator.py:821) and a parallel branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint (organization_auditlogs.py:68-83) that switches to it whenever `?optimized_pagination=true` is supplied and the caller is a superuser or has global access. Inside that branch `enable_advanced_features=True` is hardcoded, so the only gates are the new query param and the role check. None of this is related to the stated purpose of the PR, there is no justification or doc for the new endpoint flag, the new paginator has no tests, and the audit-logs branch is not tested. This should be split into a separate PR with its own description, security review, and tests.

findings.title: Negative-offset QuerySet slicing will fail at runtime, contradicting the inline comment
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment above asserts "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", but Django's docs state "Negative indexing (qs[-1]) is not supported" and the compiler translates a negative low mark directly into a SQL `OFFSET -N` clause, which is invalid SQL. The very first time an admin hits the new code path the consumer will either raise `AssertionError` from the queryset machinery or produce a database error from the generated SQL. The "advanced" path needs to be reworked to actually work (e.g. reverse ordering + a positive offset, or a count-based tail query), or removed.

findings.title: "Performance optimization" comments about negative offsets are factually wrong
findings.body: Three comments in this PR (cursors.py:26-27, paginator.py:179-181, paginator.py:874-878) claim that allowing negative cursor offsets is a "performance optimization" that enables "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning" and "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". This is incorrect: a negative offset still requires walking to that position in the result set (in SQL terms it is still an OFFSET, just expressed as a negative number). The comments advertise a benefit that the change does not deliver, which is misleading to future readers and will mislead anyone trying to reason about pagination cost.

findings.title: Hard KeyError on Kafka messages missing end_timestamp_precise
findings.body: process_batch now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"])`. The new `end_timestamp_precise` field has no default, so any incoming ingest-spans message that omits it will raise from the consumer and stall that batch. Even if the current producer always sets it, an index lookup with no `.get(..., 0.0)` fallback is fragile for a producer/consumer pipeline where the schema can evolve. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or a typed default) and let the new zset score handle missing/zero values gracefully.

findings.title: Defensive per-segment span-count cap silently removed from the flush side
findings.body: The old `_load_segment_data` aborted and dropped a segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, with an explicit metric/logger. That check is gone in the new version, so the only cap on segment size is now the insert-time `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. If the insert cap is ever bypassed (older consumer version still running, manual redis writes, or a future script change), the flusher will happily scan and ship arbitrarily large segments, with corresponding memory and downstream cost. Keep the flush-side cap (or an equivalent assertion) as a defense-in-depth bound, or add a test that exercises the case where the insert-time cap is disabled.

findings.title: Headline eviction behavior is not covered by any test
findings.body: The stated purpose of this PR is "eviction during insert": add-buffer.lua now does `zpopmin` once the segment set exceeds 1000 entries, and `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` were rewritten around sorted sets (zadd with `end_timestamp_precise` as score, zscan returning `(member, score)`). None of the existing tests in tests/sentry/spans/ exercise either behavior - no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction cap and the score ordering, and no test verifies that the score passed to zadd survives through to the flusher. A regression in the score key, the cap, or the eviction order could ship undetected.
